lesson_title: Acid Rain and the Rock That Fights Back
hook_text: The smoke from a coal power station can come back down as acid, hundreds of kilometres away.
clip_script: Coal has a little sulfur in it. Burn millions of tonnes of coal in power stations and that sulfur becomes sulfur dioxide gas. Hot engines add nitrogen oxides. These are non-metal oxides, and non-metal oxides make acids. In the clouds they turn into sulfuric and nitric acid, and the rain comes down sour, sometimes at pH 4, a hundred times more acidic than pH 6. The wind carries it hundreds of kilometres. Acid rain eats the faces off marble statues, rusts bridges, washes nutrients out of soil and kills fish in lakes. But there is a rock that fights back. Limestone is calcium carbonate, a base. Farmers spread it on sour soil to bring the pH back up for their crops. And power stations like Kusile spray their smoke with wet limestone, trapping the sulfur dioxide before it ever reaches the sky.
visual_style: Time-lapse of a cooling tower and chimney plume drifting over farmland; rain falling with a pH meter dropping; a weathered statue; a tractor spreading white lime; a scrubber diagram.
pacing: Steady build-up of the problem, a dramatic damage montage, then an upbeat solution finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn how limestone neutralises acid.
